q-138810.name: Question 1
q-138810.problem:
Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by 

$$
{y}^{′}=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x-1}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
q-138810.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x}(\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{x-1}((\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+1).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $g(x)=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+1.$

Question 1
?

Consider the function y=(ln⁡x)x. Its derivative is given by

y′=(ln⁡x)x−1⋅g(x).

Find the function g(x).

a
(ln⁡x)ln⁡(ln⁡x)+x
b
(ln⁡x)+ln⁡(ln⁡x)
c
(ln⁡x)ln⁡(ln⁡x)+1
d
(ln⁡x)ln⁡(ln⁡2x)
e
ln⁡(ln⁡x)+ln⁡x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We have the function

y=(ln⁡x)x.

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

ln⁡y=ln⁡((ln⁡x)x)ln⁡y=xln⁡(ln⁡x)

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to x:

ddx(ln⁡y)=ddx(xln⁡(ln⁡x))1y⋅y′=(x)′⋅(ln⁡(ln⁡x))+(x)⋅(ln⁡(ln⁡x))′1y⋅y′=1⋅ln⁡(ln⁡x)+x⋅(1ln⁡x⋅1x)y′y=ln⁡(ln⁡x)+1ln⁡x

Now, we solve for y′:

y′=y(ln⁡(ln⁡x)+1ln⁡x)

Finally, we substitute y=(ln⁡x)x:

y′=(ln⁡x)x(ln⁡(ln⁡x)+1ln⁡x)=(ln⁡x)x((ln⁡x)ln⁡(ln⁡x)ln⁡x+1ln⁡x)=(ln⁡x)x−1((ln⁡x)ln⁡(ln⁡x)+1).

Therefore, g(x)=(ln⁡x)ln⁡(ln⁡x)+1.

q-138841.name: Question 2
q-138841.problem:
Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
q-138841.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x))+(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+{tan}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y({sec}^{2}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+{tan}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)^{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}({sec}^{2}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+{tan}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)={sec}^{2}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)+{tan}^{2}⁡x.$

q-138841.html:
Question 2
?

Consider the function y=(sec⁡x)tan⁡x. Its derivative is given by

y′=(sec⁡x)tan⁡x⋅g(x).

Find the function g(x).

a
sec⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)+tan⁡x
b
sec2⁡xln⁡(tan⁡x)+cot2⁡x
c
tan2⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)+tan⁡x
d
sec2⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)+x
e
sec2⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)+tan2⁡x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We have the function

y=(sec⁡x)tan⁡x.

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

ln⁡y=ln⁡((sec⁡x)tan⁡x)ln⁡y=tan⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to x:

ddx(ln⁡y)=ddx(tan⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x))1y⋅y′=(tan⁡x)′⋅(ln⁡(sec⁡x))+(tan⁡x)⋅(ln⁡(sec⁡x))′1y⋅y′=sec2⁡x⋅ln⁡(sec⁡x)+tan⁡x⋅(1sec⁡x⋅tan⁡xsec⁡x)y′y=sec2⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)+tan2⁡x

Now, we solve for y′:

y′=y(sec2⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)+tan2⁡x)

Finally, we substitute y=(sec⁡x)tan⁡x:

y′=(sec⁡x)tan⁡x(sec2⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)+tan2⁡x)

Therefore, g(x)=sec2⁡xln⁡(sec⁡x)+tan2⁡x.

q-341724.name: Question 3
q-341724.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y={(\frac{1}{2x})}^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(\frac{1}{2x})}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x}))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x})+x\cdot ((2x)\cdot (-\frac{2}{(2x)^{2}})) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2x})-1 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)-1 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\frac{1}{2x})}^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-{(\frac{1}{2x})}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1) \\  & =-{(2x)}^{-x}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: ln(2x)+1

ln⁡y=ln⁡((12x)x)ln⁡y=xln⁡(12x)

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to x:

ddx(ln⁡y)=ddx(xln⁡(12x))1y⋅y′=(x)′⋅(ln⁡(12x))+(x)⋅(ln⁡(12x))′1y⋅y′=1⋅ln⁡(12x)+x⋅((2x)⋅(−2(2x)2))y′y=ln⁡(12x)−1y′y=ln⁡1−ln⁡(2x)−1y′y=−(ln⁡(2x)+1)

q-341726.name: Question 4
q-341726.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=(-7x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((-7x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{-7x}\cdot (-7)) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(-7x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(-7x)^{x}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(-7x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

q-341944.name: Question 5
q-341944.worked_solution:
The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=2$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y={(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x}))+({x}^{2})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})+{x}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})-x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =xy(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =x{(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{x})-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y={(\frac{2}{x})}^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=2} & =(2){(\frac{2}{2})}^{(2)^{2}}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{2})-1) \\  & =2(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)-1) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: −2

We have the function

ln⁡y=ln⁡((2x)x2)ln⁡y=x2ln⁡(2x)

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to x:

ddx(ln⁡y)=ddx(x2ln⁡(2x))1y⋅y′=(x2)′⋅(ln⁡(2x))+(x2)⋅(ln⁡(2x))′1y⋅y′=2x⋅ln⁡(2x)+x2⋅(−1x)y′y=2xln⁡(2x)−xy′y=x(2ln⁡(2x)−1)

Now, we solve for y′:

y′=xy(2ln⁡(2x)−1)

Finally, we substitute y=(2x)x2:

y′=x(2x)x2(2ln⁡(2x)−1)

Therefore, the slope of y=(2x)x2 at x=2 is

m=y′|x=2=(2)(22)(2)2(2ln⁡(22)−1)=2(2ln⁡(1)−1)=−2.
